stops.name: Sussex County, New Jersey: the birth of the prophet
stops.campa: On the fifth of November, in the ridge-country of Sussex, a son is born to Timothy Symmes, judge of the Common Pleas, and Mercy Harker. They give him the name of his uncle, John Cleves Symmes of the great Miami Purchase, founder of towns in the western wilderness. The boy grows grave and inward, a reader of the sky, marked from the first with the patience of a man who will one day ask the whole earth to believe him. The hollow world waits, unseen, beneath the frozen caps, for the mind that will name it.

stops.name: Ensign's commission, entry into the Army
stops.campa: Through the influence of his mighty uncle, whose lands built Cincinnati, the young man is made ensign of infantry on the twenty-sixth of March. He rides west into the service of a republic still young, into garrisons on the far rivers. He is bound for the empty places: the border forts, the Indian country, the long nights under strange stars where a soldier's mind turns over the machinery of the heavens and wonders what holds the planets true.

stops.name: Fort Adams on the Mississippi, the duel and the wounded wrist
stops.campa: At Fort Adams above Natchez, garrison talk fouls his name with a whisper against his honor over money. Symmes will not carry the slur. He faces Lieutenant Marshall on the field with pistols; both men fire and both fall wounded, and a ball tears his wrist so that his left hand is marked for life. The blood settles the quarrel; the two become friends. He has shown already the temper of the whole journey: he will pledge his body against any doubt cast upon his truth.

stops.name: New Orleans, the southern garrison
stops.campa: Stationed among the posts of the lower river, in the year of his marriage on Christmas Day to the widow Mary Anne Lockwood, mother of six, he learns the soldier's craft in the Creole heat of New Orleans. He is steady, exact, incorruptible with supplies: the very qualities that will make him press an impossible expedition upon Congress with a quartermaster's stubbornness. Promotion follows promotion: second lieutenant, first lieutenant, and at last, in the war-year 1813, captain of infantry.

stops.name: The march to the Niagara frontier
stops.campa: War calls him north. His First Infantry, long posted in the Missouri wilderness, is drawn to the Canadian border into the army of General Jacob Brown. Captain Symmes marches to the roaring frontier of Niagara, where the great falls thunder and the two flags meet. Here, in the smoke and the volley-fire, the frontier trader-to-be will earn the courage that gives his later prophecy its weight, for a man who has spiked a British gun under fire may be believed when he pledges his life to explore the pole.

stops.name: Lundy's Lane, the courage in the night battle
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of July, hard by the falls, the bloodiest field of the war is fought in the dark. Cannon flash across the ridge of Lundy's Lane; regiments grapple hand to hand among the guns until midnight. Captain Symmes stands in the storm and earns commendation for bravery, his name marked among the steadfast. The thunder of the falls and the thunder of the batteries mingle in his ears; the man who will one day speak of seas pouring into the polar verges has already stood inside the roar of the world.

stops.name: The Sortie from Fort Erie, spiking the first cannon
stops.campa: Besieged in Fort Erie, the Americans burst out in a storm of rain on the seventeenth of September to break the British siege-lines. Symmes leads his company over the entrenchments and into the battery, and with his own hand he spikes the first cannon, silencing the gun that had hammered the fort. It is his hour of pure valor, remembered ever after. The soldier who drove the spike into the enemy's iron will, four years on, drive a stranger claim into the iron certainties of the learned world.

stops.name: Honorable discharge, the soldier laid down
stops.campa: The war ended, the army reduced, Captain Symmes is honorably discharged on the fifteenth of June. He puts off the coat of the First Infantry with a wounded wrist, a spiked gun to his name, and the commendation of Lundy's Lane. Ahead lies not peace but a stranger campaign, against the whole weight of received opinion. The battlefield gives way to the frontier trading-house, and the trading-house to the lecture hall, and the lecture hall to the halls of Congress.

stops.name: The Falls of the Ohio, the frontier trader
stops.campa: At the Falls of the Ohio, where the river breaks white over its limestone shelf, the discharged captain turns trader. He learns the frontier commerce: powder, blankets, iron, the goods that move between the settlements and the wild. He watches the rivers run and the compass swing, and the old question of the garrison nights stirs again: what if the poles are not caps of ice but doorways, and the earth a shell of nested worlds? The idea gathers in him like water behind a fall.

stops.name: St. Louis, the merchant on the upper Mississippi
stops.campa: He removes to St. Louis, gateway of the far West, and under a license from Governor Clark he supplies the troops of the upper Mississippi and trades with the Fox Indians. Among the trappers and voyageurs, in the long river silences, the vision comes to its fullness. Contemplating the rings of Saturn, hollow bands nested one within another, he sees the pattern of the earth itself: solid concentric spheres, one within the other, open at the poles. The great idea is born on the Mississippi, among the peltry and the keelboats.

stops.name: St. Louis, Circular No. 1 printed and mailed to the world
stops.campa: On the tenth of April, from St. Louis, the prophecy goes out. Symmes prints five hundred copies of his Circular No. 1 and mails them to every reigning prince, every legislature, every college and philosophical society on earth, and to each member of the National Legislature, and he pins to it a physician's certificate of his sanity, that none may dismiss him as mad. The revelation of the hollow earth breaks upon the world in a single sheet of paper, signed by a late captain of infantry, of Ohio.
stops.quote: I declare the earth is hollow, and habitable within; containing a number of solid concentrick spheres, one within the other, and that it is open at the poles 12 or 16 degrees; I pledge my life in support of this truth, and am ready to explore the hollow, if the world will support and aid me in the undertaking.
stops.quote_source: John Cleves Symmes, Circular No. 1, St. Louis, Missouri Territory, April 10, 1818

stops.name: St. Louis, the call for one hundred brave companions
stops.campa: To the Circular he appends his charge and his patrons: he names Doctor Mitchill, Sir Humphry Davy, and Baron Alexander von Humboldt as protectors of his cause, and promises a treatise on the Principles of Matter. Then he asks, plainly, for the men to prove it: a hundred brave souls to set out over the ice with reindeer and sleighs, past the eighty-second degree, into the warm and stocked land within. It is the muster-roll of a voyage no man has yet dared, the first summons to the interior world.
stops.quote: I ask one hundred brave companions, well equipped, to start from Siberia in the fall season, with Reindeer and sleighs, on the ice of the frozen sea: I engage we find a warm and rich land, stocked with thrifty vegetables and animals if not men, on reaching one degree northward of latitude 82; we will return in the succeeding spring.
stops.quote_source: John Cleves Symmes, Circular No. 1, postscript, St. Louis, April 10, 1818
